viNames.name: Tép ong đỏ Crystal Red Bee

origin.fact: In 1996 the Japanese breeder Hisayasu Suzuki found one red shrimp among his black bee shrimp, and later found two more. He and other breeders then line-bred them.

Suzuki noticed slightly reddish bee shrimp in the mid-1990s. Several years of selective breeding produced the first crystal reds, and later breeders added brighter colour, sharper patterns and more white.
A German shop also credits Suzuki with first finding the red form in a tank of black bee shrimp.
A care sheet gives Taiwan as the origin.
A Vietnamese blog calls tép ong đỏ a line bred in Japan.

looks.fact: Alternating red and white bands. The whiter the shrimp, the higher the grade, and good shrimp have solid colour with clean edges between red and white.
Opacity matters: see-through patches lower the grade. A fully white shrimp grades high but cannot reach the top grade.
Grade ladder from lowest to highest: C (mostly red with thin white stripes), B (blotchy), A (opaque with defined bands), S (more white), SS (middle band reduced to a dot), SSS (most white).
C grade is the original red bee look, and SSS is also called Mosura. The name is ironic, because the shrimp is graded on its white.
Older shrimp can lose some colour or opacity but still carry the genes.
A Vietnamese shop lists grades S, SS and SSS, with some sellers adding SSSS or 'Red Ruby' for top shrimp (search snippet only; page not fetched).

lines.fact: Mosura (SSS): almost fully white body with red only on the head and tail. Sub-patterns include Flower, Crown, Heart and Smiley, named for the white mark on the red head.
Hinomaru (SS): a single red circle on top of the back. No-entry has a white dash through the dot. Double has a second dot on the tail.
S-grade patterns that can raise an S to S+: Tiger tooth (white triangle in the middle red band), V-band (middle red shaped like a triangle), and 4-band or 3-band patterns.
Pure Red Line (PRL): recommended when you want all the offspring to stay red. Ordinary crystal reds can throw black young because black is dominant.
Golden bee (white to yellow-white) is the likely source of the extra white in high-grade crystal reds. Taiwan bee strains such as Red Ruby come from a separate recessive mutation.

keeping.fact: Needs soft water with KH 0–2 and TDS of about 100–180. Use 19 L at the very least; 38 L or more is better.
In hard-water areas, use RO water with a remineralizer. Active soil is recommended. Change 10–30% of the water each week. Lives about 18–24 months. Use at least 20 L for beginners.
A Vietnamese shop gives about 50 L as the minimum tank.
Keep below about 23 °C. Above 24 °C, add aeration, because cool, oxygen-rich water suits them. A heater is often not needed.
Grazes biofilm, algae and detritus, and eats dried leaves. Feed mostly plant-based food, with extra protein for breeding.
Only tiny fish such as Otocinclus are safe tankmates. Use a shrimp-only tank for breeding.
Can live with Neocaridina and other Caridina that need similar water. Small fish such as neons are risky because they eat the young.
Use plenty of plants, moss and hiding places. Keep the water level low at first, because new shrimp may climb out. Ammonia and nitrate should be zero.

breeding.fact: Breeds readily in soft water but struggles in hard water. Females release 20–40 young about every 3–4 weeks, and adults leave the young alone.
Eggs hatch in about 28 days at 22 °C. The strongest colours develop at 24–25 °C.
A ripe female shows a saddle-shaped ovary behind the head. After moulting she releases pheromones, and she carries the eggs for about a month.
When ready to breed, females show a whitish-yellow 'yên ngựa' (saddle) on the back.
Fertile with other Caridina, and the young often keep some white. Because black is dominant, red parents can produce black young, so ordinary crystal reds do not always breed true.
Crossing with other strains can undo careful selective breeding. Breeders cross crystal black with tiger shrimp to make 'tibee'.

health.fact: Keeping KH at 0–2 lowers the risk of bad moults.
Copes poorly above 25 °C, so cooling may be needed in summer.
Line breeding has left the strain with little genetic diversity.
Sensitive to water quality. Remove uneaten food and test the water often.
A Vietnamese article says tép ong đỏ can die when temperature or pH changes.

buying.fact: A grade (opaque, with clearly defined bands) is often recommended for beginners and costs less than higher grades.
Beginners should start with a group of 10–12 low-grade crystal reds or crystal blacks.
Start with 10–20 shrimp to reduce stress.
The health of the seller's stock matters: weak shrimp are more likely to die after the move. This shrimp is fussy for beginners.
A Vietnamese article lists tép ong đỏ among the hard lines that beginners should avoid.

controversy.fact: Klotz and von Rintelen (Zootaxa, 2014) used DNA to place aquarium bee shrimp strains, crystal red among them, within Caridina cantonensis. They named the look-alike C. logemanni in the same paper, and noted possible hybridisation.
Some shops still sell crystal red as Caridina logemanni, which conflicts with the DNA findings.
The related, heavily line-bred Taiwan bee strains are described as highly inbred and prone to genetic defects and deformities.
